stories.headline: OIL SPIKES ABOVE $83 ON IRAN IMPASSE, FADES TO $82 BY SETTLEMENT AS STRAIT OF HORMUZ STANDOFF DRAGS ON
stories.body: WTI crude touched above $83 a barrel intraday as Iran reiterated it will keep the Strait of Hormuz shut until its demands are met, before settling near $81.99, down about 0.2% on the day. The intraday round-trip left a persistent risk premium embedded in the forward curve even as the spot price cooled.
stories.explain: Roughly a fifth of global seaborne crude transits the Strait of Hormuz, so any escalation in the standoff forces traders to bid up near-dated contracts faster than the market can confirm whether flows are actually at risk — that's why the intraday spike outran the eventual settlement. The fade back to $82 doesn't mean the risk is gone; it means the premium shifted from a panic bid into the futures curve itself, which is exactly the kind of embedded volatility that can resurface hard if Wednesday's CPI print or fresh Iran headlines break the wrong way.

stories.headline: MARKETS BRACE FOR WEDNESDAY'S CPI, WITH HEADLINE SEEN COOLING TO 3.4% BUT CORE EXPECTED TO REBOUND
stories.body: The Bureau of Labor Statistics releases July CPI Wednesday at 8:30 AM ET, with headline inflation expected to ease to 3.4% year-over-year from June's 3.5%, while core CPI is forecast to rebound to +0.24% month-over-month after June's flat core reading. It's the last major data point before the September FOMC meeting.
stories.explain: The split matters more than either number alone: a cooling headline paired with a firming core would suggest June's soft core print was noise rather than a trend, which is the scenario the Fed's hawks — including voters pushing back on rate-cut bets — would seize on to argue disinflation is stalling. With oil's Strait of Hormuz premium sitting in the background, any upside surprise in the energy or core-goods components gets read as confirmation that geopolitical risk is starting to bleed into realized inflation, not just headline optics.

stories.headline: S&P 500 SLIPS 0.06% TO 7,753, NASDAQ 100 FALLS 0.40% AS ALPHABET SINKS AND TRADERS DE-RISK AHEAD OF CPI
stories.body: The S&P 500 closed at 7,753.11, down 0.06%, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.40% to roughly 29,503 as Alphabet shares sank and the US-Iran impasse kept a lid on risk appetite. Bending Spoons surged 15.7% ahead of its Q2 earnings and Datadog jumped 11.5% on a strong quarter and analyst upgrades.
stories.explain: The divergence between a resilient S&P and a weaker Nasdaq 100 signals investors are trimming exposure to the most rate- and growth-sensitive megacap tech names specifically, not de-risking broadly — consistent with positioning ahead of a CPI print that could move the September rate-cut odds that those richly-valued names are most sensitive to. Idiosyncratic earnings winners like Datadog and Bending Spoons show stock-picking is still rewarded even in a cautious tape, which is a useful signal that this is a positioning pause, not a broad risk-off move.

stories.headline: TREASURY YIELDS TICK UP TO 4.73% ON THE 10-YEAR AS TRADERS POSITION AHEAD OF INFLATION DATA
stories.body: The 10-year Treasury yield rose about 2 bps to 4.73% while the 2-year traded near 4.24%, with both ends of the curve edging higher as investors positioned defensively ahead of Wednesday's CPI release rather than committing to a directional bet.
stories.explain: A small, roughly parallel move across the curve — rather than a sharp front-end swing — signals the market isn't repricing Fed policy expectations yet; it's raising the term premium slightly to compensate for the binary uncertainty of tomorrow's data. That's the bond market equivalent of buying insurance: yields drift a touch higher into the event because a hot core print would force a faster repricing than a cool one, and the curve wants to be positioned for either outcome rather than caught flat-footed.

stories.headline: GOLD SLIPS BELOW $4,400 AS PROFIT-TAKING AND A FIRMER DOLLAR OFFSET SAFE-HAVEN DEMAND
stories.body: Gold fell to about $4,367 an ounce, down 0.55%, giving back part of a recent rally as the dollar index firmed slightly to 99.84 and traders locked in gains after a month that has still seen gold rise more than 9%.
stories.explain: Gold is caught between two competing flows today: geopolitical and inflation-hedge demand tied to the Iran standoff and tomorrow's CPI, and a stronger dollar that makes gold more expensive for foreign buyers and reduces its relative appeal versus yield-bearing Treasuries. The pullback shows the profit-taking impulse won out today, but with gold still up over 30% year-over-year, the underlying hedging bid hasn't disappeared — it's just paused into the CPI print, the same way equities and bonds are.

stories.headline: COURT DENIES NCAA'S BID TO STAY ELIGIBILITY INJUNCTION AS NEW LAWSUIT ADDS MIAMI'S MALIK RENEAU, SOUTH CAROLINA'S MIKE SHARAVJAMTS
stories.body: A federal judge in Colorado denied the NCAA's motion to stay the preliminary injunction granting blanket fifth-year eligibility to athletes who began competing in 2022-23, and a fresh lawsuit filed in South Carolina by 17 football and men's basketball players — including Miami's Malik Reneau and South Carolina's Mike Sharavjamts — seeks to extend the same relief. Rosters across both sports remain in flux with the season 82 days out.

stories.headline: LEBRON JAMES SIGNS WITH 76ERS AFTER EIGHT SEASONS WITH THE LAKERS
stories.body: LeBron James agreed to join the Philadelphia 76ers in one of the biggest free agency moves of the offseason, ending an eight-year run in Los Angeles. Separately, Draymond Green re-signed with the Warriors on a one-year, $27.7M deal, and the NBA will unveil its full 2026-27 schedule Thursday at 3 PM ET on ESPN2.

stories.headline: TRAINING CAMP INJURY WAVE HITS LIONS AND JETS AS SEASON OPENERS DRAW NEAR
stories.body: The Detroit Lions lost starting center Cade Mays to a hand fracture and running back Isiah Pacheco to a torn MCL, while Jets CB Qwan'tez Stiggers was hospitalized after collapsing at practice, with his condition not yet disclosed. Elsewhere, Saints DE Cameron Jordan could open the season on the shelf with a hamstring injury.

stories.headline: PORTAL TREND: COACHES BRING THEIR OWN PLAYERS TO NEW PROGRAMS AS 2026 CAMPS OPEN
stories.body: New Oklahoma State coach Eric Morris brought 21 former North Texas players, including 4,379-yard passer Drew Mestemaker; Kyle Whittingham took Utah pass rusher John Henry Daley with him to Michigan; and new Penn State coach Matt Campbell's roster includes about two dozen former Iowa State players, led by QB Rocco Becht. Of 14,070 portal entrants this cycle, 3,685 hit the portal with 76% already committed.

sports.detail: Second week of fall camp underway in Seattle, with the defense a step ahead of the offense — interceptions in each of the last two practices — and DL Ta'ita'i Uiagalelei back on the field for Day 3 in pads. Season opener vs. Washington State (Apple Cup) is Sunday, Sept. 6, Husky Stadium.

UW loses top scorer Hannes Steinbach (drafted 14th overall by Charlotte) and No. 2 scorer Zoom Diallo (transferred to Kentucky); Wesley Yates III returns as the leading scoring option. Danny Sprinkle added Rutgers transfer Harun Zrno and NBA veteran Charles Klask to the staff as the Huskies rebuild in Year 2 of the Big Ten.

HBO's Hard Knocks premieres tonight, 9 PM PT, following Seahawks camp for five weeks. Seattle signed LB Aaron Smith and placed FB Robbie Ouzts on IR; S Nick Emmanwori passed his physical and is off PUP. Preseason opener vs. Dallas is Saturday, Aug. 15, 5 PM PT, Lumen Field.

Restricted free agent Jalen Duren remains unsigned more than a month into free agency; Detroit has offered $35-38M per year while Duren is seeking a max deal north of $40M annually. No offer sheet from a rival has emerged, and reports suggest a rocky 2026 playoff showing has cooled the front office's urgency to pay him.

Seattle opens a series at Yankee Stadium tonight, 7:05 PM ET, looking to rebound after being swept by Tampa Bay over the weekend. The Mariners remain in a tight AL West race a handful of games back of Houston.

watchlist: CPI report — Wednesday, Aug. 12, 8:30 AM ET — headline seen cooling to 3.4% YoY, but core expected to rebound to +0.24% MoM
Mariners at Yankees — Tuesday, Aug. 11, 7:05 PM ET, Yankee Stadium
NBA full 2026-27 schedule release — Thursday, Aug. 13, 3 PM ET, ESPN2
Seahawks preseason opener vs. Cowboys — Saturday, Aug. 15, 5 PM PT, Lumen Field

deepDive.title: The Anatomy of a Geopolitical Risk Premium: Why WTI Spiked Above $83 and Faded Back to $82
content: Today's oil price action is a clean case study in how geopolitical risk gets priced into a commodity in real time. WTI opened near $82.34, spiked above $83 intraday as Iran reiterated it would keep the Strait of Hormuz shut, then settled near $81.99 — down about 0.2% on the day despite the scary headline. That round-trip isn't noise; it's the market processing new information faster than the underlying supply situation actually changes, which is exactly how risk premia get built and unwound within a single session.

The mechanism runs through the futures curve, not just the spot price. When a chokepoint carrying roughly a fifth of global seaborne crude is threatened, traders don't wait to confirm actual barrels are stranded — they bid up near-dated contracts on the probability-weighted chance of disruption, and options desks see call skew widen as buyers pay up for upside protection. As the session wears on and no confirmed supply disruption materializes, some of that panic bid unwinds, even though the underlying standoff hasn't been resolved. The premium doesn't vanish; it migrates from the spot price into the shape of the curve itself.

This is the same dynamic that played out during the 1990 Gulf War spike and, more recently, in 2022 after Russia's invasion of Ukraine: an initial overshoot on headline risk, followed by partial normalization once traders can assess actual flow disruption versus rhetorical escalation. The tell is usually the futures curve's shape — a standoff that's genuinely worsening tends to show backwardation deepening (near-term contracts pricing well above later ones) even as spot cools, signaling the market still expects near-term scarcity even if today's headline number looks calmer.

For Wednesday's CPI, this matters directly: energy is roughly 6-7% of the CPI basket, and it's the multi-day average price that feeds into the inflation calculation, not a single intraday spike or a single settlement. A one-day fade to $82 doesn't erase the fact that oil has been elevated for four straight sessions on this standoff. If Iran headlines escalate again before Thursday's pump-price data gets baked into the following month's report, today's round-trip could easily repeat itself — and each repeat keeps a floor under the energy component the Fed will be watching closely.
